reducing-ozone-depletion-s1.title: Timeline of ozone depletion and the Montreal Protocol

reducing-ozone-depletion-s2.title: A town debates its old refrigerators
reducing-ozone-depletion-s2.passage: CFC production has ended, yet our job is not done. Thousands of refrigerators, freezers and air conditioners made before the 1990s are still in basements and garages across town, each holding a charge of CFC refrigerant. When these machines are crushed at the scrapyard without first draining the refrigerant, the gas escapes into the air and begins its slow trip to the stratosphere. Capturing it costs a few dollars per appliance. Leaving it costs the ozone layer.

items.q: What did the Montreal Protocol, signed in 1987, do?
options: It phased out CFCs and other ozone-depleting chemicals
It set limits on carbon dioxide emissions from power plants
It banned the trade of endangered animals and their parts
It required cars to use catalytic converters

why.correct: The Montreal Protocol is an international treaty that phased out the production of CFCs, halons and other ozone-depleting substances.
options: Right: it is the treaty that ended most production of ozone-depleting chemicals.
Carbon dioxide limits are the subject of climate agreements, not the Montreal Protocol.
That describes a wildlife trade treaty, not the Montreal Protocol.
Catalytic converters were required by national air pollution laws, not this treaty.

items.q: Why were HCFCs used as replacements for CFCs, and why are they being phased out too?
options: They contain no chlorine, but they are toxic to breathe
They destroy less ozone, but still contain some chlorine
They make more ozone than CFCs destroy, so they are too strong
They are cheaper than CFCs, but they cause acid rain

why.correct: HCFCs were a stopgap: less ozone-depleting than CFCs, not harmless. They are being phased out on a later schedule.
options: HCFCs do contain chlorine; that is why they still deplete some ozone.
Right: HCFCs break down lower in the atmosphere, so less chlorine reaches the stratosphere, but some does.
HCFCs do not make ozone.
Acid rain comes from NOx and SOx, not HCFCs.

items.q: HFCs replaced many CFCs and HCFCs in air conditioners. Which statement describes a drawback of HFCs?
options: They destroy ozone faster than the CFCs they replaced
They do not work as refrigerants in air conditioners
They spare ozone but trap far more heat than CO₂
They are banned by the original 1987 Montreal Protocol

why.correct: Solving one problem created another: HFCs protect ozone but warm the climate, so the 2016 Kigali Amendment phases them down.
options: HFCs contain no chlorine or bromine, so they do not destroy ozone.
HFCs work well as refrigerants; that is why they spread.
Right: HFCs contain no chlorine, but many are powerful heat-trapping gases.
HFCs were added later, by the Kigali Amendment of 2016.

items.q: According to the timeline, how many years passed between the Montreal Protocol and the end of CFC production worldwide?
options: 9 years
36 years
79 years
23 years

why.correct: Developed countries stopped by 1996 and developing countries had until 2010: $2010 - 1987 = 23$ years.
options: That is the gap from 1987 to 1996, when developed countries ended production.
That is the gap from 1974, the first warning, to 2010.
That is the gap from 1987 to the expected recovery around 2066.
Right: 2010 − 1987 = 23 years.

items.q: Why does the timeline show recovery of Antarctic ozone around 2066, decades after CFC production ended?
options: CFCs already released last for decades
Countries are still allowed to make CFCs until 2066
The ozone layer needs new CFCs to rebuild itself
UV light will stop reaching the stratosphere in 2066

why.correct: Recovery lags production cuts because CFCs are long-lived.
options: Right: CFCs last 50 to 100 years or more, so their chlorine keeps destroying ozone.
Production ended worldwide by 2010.
CFCs destroy ozone; they do not rebuild it.
UV keeps reaching the stratosphere; that is how ozone forms.

items.q: Scientists first warned about CFCs in 1974, and Antarctic ozone is expected back to 1980 levels around 2066. How many years separate the warning and the expected recovery?

why.correct: $2066 - 1974 = 92$ years: almost a century from warning to recovery.

mistakes.why: That counts from the Montreal Protocol (1987). The question starts at the first warning, 1974.
1980 is the ozone level used as the target, not the year of the warning. Use 2066 − 1974.

items.q: What does the timeline suggest about why the Montreal Protocol is seen as a success?
options: Ozone recovered fully within a year of the treaty
CFCs were found to be harmless after the treaty
Quick action, and ozone is on track to recover
The treaty was signed before anyone had measured ozone loss

why.correct: From the 1974 warning to the 1987 treaty took 13 years; with every UN member taking part, ozone-depleting substances fell sharply and recovery is under way.
options: Recovery is expected to take until about 2066.
CFCs do destroy ozone; that is why they were phased out.
Right: quick, worldwide action, then measured recovery.
The ozone hole was reported in 1985, two years before the treaty.

items.q: What is the author’s main claim?
options: CFCs are still made in large amounts by most countries
The ozone layer has already fully recovered
New refrigerators should use CFCs again
CFCs in old appliances must be captured at disposal

why.correct: The claim is about the "bank" of CFCs still sealed in old appliances and foam.
options: The passage says production has ended; the problem is CFCs already in equipment.
The passage says recovery is under way, not complete.
The passage argues for capturing CFCs, not using them again.
Right: the passage argues that CFCs in old equipment are a remaining source.

items.q: Which assumption does the argument depend on?
options: Uncaptured refrigerant escapes when appliances are crushed
People will stop buying new refrigerators
CFCs break down quickly once they leave an appliance
Landfills absorb the CFCs that reach them

why.correct: The need for capture assumes the gas escapes otherwise.
options: Right: the argument only works if CFCs escape when appliances are scrapped carelessly.
The argument is about disposal, not about buying less.
If they broke down quickly, capturing them would not matter.
If landfills held them, there would be no need for capture.

items.q: Which evidence would best support the author’s claim?
options: A survey showing most people like their new refrigerators
Measured CFC leaks at scrapyards that crush appliances
Data showing CFC production ended worldwide by 2010
A report that ozone holes are smaller in some years

why.correct: Evidence should connect the proposed source (old appliances) to actual emissions.
options: Opinions about new refrigerators do not test the claim.
Right: direct evidence that the bank is leaking supports the call for capture.
That is background; the claim is about CFCs already in equipment.
Year-to-year changes in the hole do not show where CFCs come from.

items.q: Propose a policy that would reduce CFC release from old appliances in the town in the passage.

why.correct: A policy is a law or rule. A full answer says what it requires and how that protects ozone.

policy.label: Policy or technology
options: a town law
a recovery machine
a new refrigerator design

why.1: A machine is a technology. A policy is a law or rule that requires an action.
why.2: A design is a technology, not a policy.

rule.label: What it requires
options: scrapyards to remove and capture refrigerant before crushing appliances
residents to keep their old refrigerators forever
stores to sell more air conditioners

why.1: Appliances wear out; the rule must deal with them at disposal.
why.2: Selling more appliances does not keep CFCs out of the air.

mechanism.label: How it works
options: keeps the CFCs out of the air so they cannot reach the stratosphere
makes the CFCs break down into ozone
cools the stratosphere

why.1: CFCs do not turn into ozone.
why.2: The goal is to keep chlorine out of the stratosphere, not to change its temperature.

specific.model: Pass a town law that requires scrapyards to remove and capture the refrigerant from old appliances before crushing them, because it keeps the CFCs out of the air, so they cannot reach the stratosphere and release chlorine that destroys ozone.

items.q: Which replacement refrigerant neither depletes ozone nor traps much heat?
options: CFC-12, used in refrigerators before the 1990s
HCFC-22, used in older air conditioners
Halons, used in fire extinguishers
Isobutane, used in many new refrigerators

why.correct: Hydrocarbons such as isobutane and propane, ammonia and carbon dioxide are alternatives with no ozone depletion and little warming.
options: CFC-12 is a CFC; it destroys ozone.
HCFC-22 contains chlorine and depletes some ozone.
Halons contain bromine, which destroys ozone strongly.
Right: hydrocarbons contain no chlorine and have very low warming effects, though they are flammable.

items.q: Which actions reduce ozone depletion? Select all that apply.
options: Phasing out the production of CFCs and halons
Capturing refrigerant when old air conditioners are scrapped
Installing scrubbers on coal-burning power plants
Planting trees to absorb carbon dioxide

why.correct: Only actions that keep chlorine and bromine compounds out of the stratosphere reduce ozone depletion.
options: Right: that is the core of the Montreal Protocol.
Right: it keeps CFCs already in use out of the air.
Scrubbers remove sulfur dioxide, an acid-rain gas, not ozone-depleting substances.
Carbon dioxide does not destroy stratospheric ozone.

items.q: A country used 120,000 metric tons of CFCs a year before the Montreal Protocol and 6,000 metric tons a year a decade later. Write the setup for the percent change, then the answer.

mistakes.why: Divide by the old value, 120,000 metric tons, not the new value.
Use new minus old: use fell, so the change is negative.
You forgot to multiply by 100: −0.95 as a percent is −95%.

items.q: Which feature of the Montreal Protocol most helped it work worldwide?
options: Each country chose its own goals with no deadlines
It applied to the United States and Europe alone
Extra time and funds for developing countries
It allowed CFC use to continue in spray cans

why.correct: Phase-out schedules, help from the Multilateral Fund and later deadlines for developing countries brought universal participation.
options: The treaty set firm phase-out schedules.
Every UN member state ratified it.
Right: a fund and later deadlines helped every country take part.
CFC uses were phased out, including spray cans.

items.q: A policy question asks for a way to protect the ozone layer. Which answer names a policy rather than a technology?
options: Refrigerators that use isobutane instead of CFCs
Machines that recover refrigerant from old air conditioners
Foam insulation made without ozone-depleting gases
A law banning new products made with HCFCs

why.correct: A policy is a law, rule, tax or treaty. Technologies can be part of a policy, but the answer must name the rule.
options: That is a technology; a policy would require or reward it.
That is a technology; a policy would require its use.
That is a product, not a policy.
Right: a law or rule is a policy.
